analysis.one_liner: Cuts income tax rates to as low as 10%, simplifies filing, and pays for it by closing tax breaks for investors and corporations.
analysis.headline: The House Democratic Leader's tax cut bill drew zero cosponsors, went to four committees, and died without a hearing or vote when the 105th Congress ended in January 1999.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have cut income tax rates across the board, with a new 10% rate on the first slice of income, a bigger standard deduction, a bigger personal exemption, and an end to the marriage penalty. To pay for it, it would have taken away tax breaks that mostly flow to investors and corporations: it would tax interest on municipal bonds, repeal most itemized deductions, tax employer-provided perks, and create a commission to shut down federal corporate subsidies. It also would have required a national vote before any future income tax rate increase, and pushed the IRS toward a system where most people wouldn't have to file a return at all.
analysis.who_benefits: Working and middle-income families would get lower rates, a 10% bottom rate, a larger standard deduction ($9,000 for joint filers), a larger personal exemption ($2,900 with the phaseout repealed), and the marriage penalty eliminated in both rates and deductions. Everyone who finds filing painful would benefit from a planned return-free system. Taxpayers generally would benefit from a new commission designed to identify and terminate corporate subsidies, with fast-track procedures to force a vote on its recommendations.

how_it_helps.text: Replaces the current rates with a schedule starting at 10% on the first $23,000-$46,000 of taxable income (depending on filing status), and cuts the top rate to 34%.

Raises the standard deduction to $9,000 for joint filers and $4,500 for singles, raises the personal exemption to $2,900 and repeals its phaseout for high earners, and eliminates the marriage penalty in both rates and the deduction.
Cuts the alternative minimum tax rates from 26%/28% to 19%/21%.

Repeals nearly all itemized deductions (keeping only mortgage interest, investment interest, and work expenses), which today mostly benefit higher-income filers, and makes investment interest and work expenses deductible above the line so all filers can claim them.

Creates a Corporate Subsidy Reform Commission to identify federal payments and tax advantages that give companies unfair windfalls, and includes expedited procedures forcing Congress to vote on an implementing bill.
Directs Treasury to develop a return-free filing system for as many taxpayers as practicable, so most people would no longer have to prepare their own tax return.

analysis.who_pays: Municipal bond investors and state and local governments would lose the tax exemption on newly issued bonds. Corporations receiving federal subsidies could see them terminated. Workers would lose the tax exclusion for employer-provided benefits other than health insurance — including dependent care assistance, education assistance, and the tax deferral on employer retirement contributions — and would no longer be able to contribute to a Roth IRA. Higher-income filers would lose most itemized deductions, and taxpayers abroad would lose the foreign earned income exclusion.
analysis.who_pays_short: Bond investors, subsidized corporations, workers with employer benefits

drawbacks.text: The bill pays for rate cuts partly by taxing things working families use: it would make employer-paid dependent care assistance, education assistance, and other fringe benefits taxable, end the tax-free treatment of employer retirement contributions, and repeal the dependent care credit and the credit for the elderly and disabled.
Ending the tax exemption for new municipal bonds would raise borrowing costs for state and local governments, which could mean higher taxes or fewer services at the local level.
Ending tax deferral on 401(k)-style contributions and terminating the Roth IRA would disrupt retirement saving for workers who rely on it.
Requiring a national referendum before any income tax rate increase is an untested mechanism with constitutional questions, and could make ordinary tax policy impossible to adjust.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is real: lower rates and simpler filing for ordinary families, paid for by narrowing tax breaks that skew toward investors, corporations, and higher earners. But the bill asks workers to give up some benefits they use every day — pre-tax dependent care accounts, education assistance, and tax-deferred retirement contributions — to fund cuts that also lower the top rate for high earners. Whether a given family came out ahead would depend heavily on which benefits they used; a two-earner family with a pre-tax childcare account and a 401(k) could lose as much as it gained. The referendum requirement and the corporate subsidy commission are untested and would have added significant uncertainty.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to four committees the day it was introduced, its tax provisions landed in the Ways and Means Committee, no hearing or vote ever happened, and the bill died when the 105th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Richard Gephardt, the House Minority Leader, introduced the bill on April 1, 1998 as his signature tax proposal.
No member of either party cosponsored it.
It was referred the same day to four committees — Ways and Means, Rules, Government Reform and Oversight, and House Oversight — with the tax provisions going to Ways and Means.

The only further action was a routine subcommittee referral in the Government Reform committee on April 7, 1998; no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever occurred before the Congress ended on January 3, 1999.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Industries that would have lost their tax advantages — municipal bond investors, corporations receiving federal subsidies, and the tax-preparation business — kept the status quo, as did workers with tax-free employer benefits who would have paid more. Ordinary families did not get the rate cuts, the marriage penalty fix, or return-free filing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Bond investors, subsidized corporations, and tax preparers

for.name: Richard Gephardt
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its sole sponsor.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: The tax-writing committee, chaired by a Republican, where all tax bills start
against.what_they_did: Never held a hearing or acted on the bill after referral.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.role: Speaker and majority party of the 105th House
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to four committees simultaneously, a route that typically stalls a bill; no committee ever considered it.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never got a vote, so there is no roll-call to judge; it had one sponsor, a Democrat, and zero cosponsors from either party.

industries.note: The bill creates a commission to identify and terminate federal subsidies and tax advantages that give businesses unfair windfalls, with procedures forcing a congressional vote. These subsidies are public money flowing to private companies.
Interest on bonds issued after 1998 would become taxable, ending a subsidy whose benefits flow mainly to high-bracket investors; state and local governments would face higher borrowing costs.

Employers could no longer offer pre-tax cafeteria plans, tuition reductions, dependent care assistance, or other tax-free perks other than health coverage. The cost would land largely on the workers who use these benefits.

Employer retirement contributions would be taxed up front, Roth IRAs would be closed to new contributions, and pre-tax retirement saving deductions would be repealed, shrinking the tax-deferral business.
A return-free filing system for most taxpayers would eliminate a large share of paid preparation and software revenue while saving ordinary filers time and money.
The exclusion for foreign earned income would be repealed, raising taxes on citizens working abroad.
